newsitem.title: ITALY: Jerusalem will make or break Mideast peace - Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem will make or break Mideast peace - Arafat.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Thursday that his landmark meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was positive but that the issue of Jerusalem would either make or break Middle East peace.

"This was a positive meeting that we hope will reinforce the process of peace between Arabs and Israelis and peace in the whole region," Arafat said in a speech to Rome community leaders, including Jews.
Arafat met Netanyahu for the first time on Wednesday for a brief summit on the Israel-Gaza border to relaunch stalled talks on extending Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza.

Though they did not solve major problems, the meeting and a reserved handshake were seen as vital symbols of both sides' commitment to the Oslo agreement signed with the PLO by the Labour government which right-winger Netanyahu toppled in May.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who was also in Rome on Thursday but did not meet Arafat, said the Jewish state would continue the peace process while safeguarding its own security.

In his speech at Rome's city hall, Arafat took a firm stand on Jerusalem, saying the issue of its status "could either make the peace process fall or become a symbol of co-existence and harmony between Moslems, Christians and Jews".
"To insist in saying that Jerusalem is the capital of Israel is a fact that is contrary to truth and reality, besides being a violation of a (U.N.) resolution and international law."
Israel declared Jerusalem its "united and eternal" capital in 1980, 13 years after its forces captured the city's Arab eastern sector from Jordan in the Six-Day War.
Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Its fate is up for negotiation at final peace talks.
"We want Jerusalem to be an open city, capital of two people, the Palestinian people and the Israeli people," Arafat said.

The encounter was attended by leaders of the Italian and Roman Jewish communities, some of whom did not applaud when Arafat entered and left the frescoed room and remained stony-faced when he spoke of Jerusalem.
The Jewish community vividly remembers a 1982 Palestinian guerrilla attack on a Rome synagogue that killed a boy aged two.

The union of young Italian Jews asked Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who also met Arafat, to press him to hand over a Palestinian who was convicted in his absence in 1988 to life imprisonment for the synagogue attack.
Arafat began his 12-hour visit to Rome at the Vatican, where he held talks with Pope John Paul's two top diplomats, Cardinal Angelo Sodano and Archbishop Jean-Louis Tauran.
The Vatican did not say why Arafat did not meet the Pope, who is at his summer palace south of Rome ahead of a weekend trip to Hungary. They have met several times in the past.

A Vatican statement said Arafat and Sodano had cordial talks, which covered the "existing difficulties" in peace negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian Authority and "the delicate problem" of Jerusalem.
The Vatican wants international guarantees protecting Jerusalem as a city sacred to Moslems, Christians and Jews. Israel says the city's holy places are open to all believers.
Most states, including the Vatican, have not recognised Jerusalem as the Jewish state's capital and keep their embassies elsewhere, mostly in Tel Aviv and its suburbs.
Arafat was flying north later on Thursday for an international business forum at the resort of Cernobbio. It will also be attended by former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres.
